issue: Source: "a resistance in which they will be supported by constitutional and patriotic principles" (pronoun "they" left ambiguous by Hamilton/Madison). Candidate resolves it by inserting "the House" ("principles will back the House"), an interpretive addition. Keep the source pronoun.
replacement: But will not the House of Representatives be as much interested as the Senate in keeping the government working as it should? Will it not therefore be unwilling to risk the government's existence or reputation on the Senate's giving way? Or, if such a test of firmness between the two branches were risked, would one not be as likely as the other to yield first? These questions will give no trouble to those who reflect that in every case, the smaller the number of men in power and the more lasting and conspicuous their position, the stronger the interest each of them will feel individually in whatever concerns the government. Those who represent the dignity of their country in the eyes of other nations will be especially aware of every prospect of public danger or of dishonorable stagnation in public affairs. We must ascribe to these causes the continual triumph of the British House of Commons over the other branches of the government whenever it has used the engine of a money bill. Absolute inflexibility on the part of those other branches would have thrown every department of the state into general confusion. It has neither been feared nor experienced. The greatest firmness the federal Senate or President can show will be no more than equal to a resistance in which they will be backed by constitutional and patriotic principles.

issue: Two small changes: (1) source "at least as many different periods as there are months" -> candidate drops "at least"; (2) source "may be found by experience to be of great importance ... both as a security against ... and as a cure for the diseases of faction" -> candidate turns it into flat assertions "It guards against ... and it cures the diseases of faction", sharpening the claim.
replacement: So far my observations have aimed only at defending the provision in question on three grounds: theoretical propriety, the danger of placing the power elsewhere, and the safety of placing it as proposed. But I must mention one more thing, a positive advantage that will result from this arrangement and that could not as well have been obtained from any other. I mean the uniformity in the time of elections for the federal House of Representatives. It is more than possible that experience will prove this uniformity of great importance to the public welfare. It may prove important both as a security against the perpetuation of the same spirit in the body and as a cure for the diseases of faction. If each State may choose its own time of election, there may be at least as many different times as there are months in the year. The times of election in the individual States, as now fixed for local purposes, range between extremes as far apart as March and November. The result of this diversity would be that the body could never be entirely dissolved or renewed at one time. If an improper spirit of any kind happened to prevail in it, that spirit would tend to pass itself on to the new members as they arrived in succession. The mass would probably stay nearly the same, constantly absorbing its gradual additions into itself. There is a contagion in example that few men have the strength of mind to resist. I am inclined to think that three times the term in office, on condition that the whole body is dissolved at once, might be less dangerous to liberty than one third of that term with gradual and successive changes.

issue: Source "a practice subversive of all the principles of order and regular government" -> candidate "It destroys every principle", stronger than "subversive of".
replacement: Related to the objection about the number of representatives, and properly noted here, is another objection, about the number needed to conduct legislative business. It has been said that a quorum should have required more than a majority, and that in particular cases, if not in all, a decision should have required more than a majority of a quorum. It cannot be denied that such a precaution might have brought some advantages. It might have been an additional shield for some particular interests, and a further general obstacle to hasty and biased measures. But the drawbacks on the other side outweigh these considerations. Whenever justice or the general good might require new laws or active measures, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. The majority would no longer rule; power would pass to the minority. Suppose this protective privilege were limited to particular cases. A self-interested minority might use it to shield themselves from fair sacrifices for the general welfare, or, in particular emergencies, to extort unreasonable concessions. Lastly, it would make easy and encourage the harmful practice of secession. This practice has appeared even in States where only a majority is required. It undermines every principle of order and regular government, and it leads more directly to public convulsions and the ruin of popular governments than any other practice yet seen among us.
